concepts.name: Restoration and Expansion of Legislative Council under Act of 1861
key_dimensions: Why the legislative council was abolished after 1857 and the political context of its restoration
Composition: addition of non-official members (both Indian and European) to the Viceroy's Executive Council for legislative purposes
Distinction between the Executive Council (governing body) and the expanded Legislative Council (law-making body) — a frequent UPSC trap
Minimum and maximum membership limits (6 to 12 additional members) and their nominated nature

concepts.name: Portfolio System Introduced by Act of 1861
key_dimensions: Formal codification of the portfolio system — distribution of government departments among Executive Council members
Role of Lord Canning in informally initiating the system before 1861 and its statutory recognition
Comparison with Cabinet system in Britain — similarities and critical differences (no collective responsibility in India)
Significance as a step toward administrative rationalization rather than representative governance

concepts.name: Viceroy's Power of Ordinance under Act of 1861
key_dimensions: Provision allowing the Viceroy to promulgate ordinances without legislative council approval during emergencies
Validity period of ordinances (6 months) — a commonly tested specific detail
Comparison with later ordinance-making powers under GoI Acts of 1909, 1919, 1935
Constitutional continuity: how this power evolved into Article 123 of the Indian Constitution

concepts.name: Decentralization of Legislative Powers: Provincial Councils under 1861 Act
key_dimensions: Re-activation of legislative councils in Bombay and Madras Presidencies (abolished in 1833) — reversal of centralization trend of 1833
Creation of new legislative councils for Bengal, North-Western Provinces, and Punjab
Limitations: provincial councils could not override central legislation; Viceroy held veto
Significance as the first formal move toward legislative federalism in India

concepts.name: Nominated Non-Official Members: Nature and Limitations (1861)
key_dimensions: Non-official members were nominated by the Viceroy, not elected — distinction critical for UPSC
Inclusion of Indians as nominated members for the first time (e.g., Raja Dinkur Rao, Sir Dinkar Rao)
Non-official members had no power to ask questions, move resolutions, or vote on the budget
Contrast with the 1892 Act's quasi-representative reforms to understand incremental change

concepts.name: Prohibition on Legislative Council Discussing Certain Matters (1861)
key_dimensions: Legislative councils could not discuss public affairs, finances, or budget — strictly law-making bodies
No right to interpellation or questioning the executive — sharp contrast with Westminster model
This restriction as a deliberate colonial policy to prevent any form of popular accountability
How 1892 Act partially addressed this by allowing limited budget discussion

concepts.name: Introduction of Limited Election Principle under Act of 1892
key_dimensions: The word 'election' was not used in the 1892 Act — members were 'nominated on recommendation' of bodies like municipalities, district boards, universities, chambers of commerce
UPSC trap: 1892 did NOT introduce direct elections; it introduced the principle of representation through indirect/recommendatory mechanism
Which bodies had the right to recommend members — distinction between official and non-official recommendatory bodies
Comparison with the fully elective principle introduced by Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)

concepts.name: Expansion of Legislative Council Membership under 1892 Act
key_dimensions: Increase in the number of additional members in the Central Legislative Council (maximum raised to 16)
Expansion of provincial legislative councils with more non-official members
Non-official members still remained a minority — official majority retained as a colonial safeguard
Significance of the official majority principle and when it was finally abolished (1919 provincial councils)

concepts.name: Right to Discuss Budget under Act of 1892
key_dimensions: 1892 Act allowed members to discuss (but NOT vote on) the annual budget — a landmark incremental reform
Distinction: discussion ≠ voting rights — UPSC frequently tests this nuance
Contrast with 1861 Act where even discussion of budget was prohibited
Evolution: full voting rights on budget came only with Government of India Act 1919

concepts.name: Right of Interpellation (Questions) under Act of 1892
key_dimensions: Members were allowed to ask questions to the executive for the first time — foundational parliamentary practice
Limitations: prior notice required, presiding officer could disallow questions, no supplementary questions allowed
Contrast with modern parliamentary question hour — no right to supplementary questions was a critical restriction
Significance as the origin of legislative oversight of the executive in Indian constitutional history

concepts.name: Role of Indian National Congress in Pressuring the 1892 Reforms
key_dimensions: INC (founded 1885) formally demanded expansion of councils and introduction of elections at early sessions
The 1892 Act as a direct British response to mounting nationalist pressure — significance of extra-parliamentary agitation
Why British concessions were limited: fear of representative government leading to self-rule
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and moderate Congress leaders' differing assessments of the 1892 Act's adequacy

concepts.name: Official Majority Principle: Retention as Colonial Safeguard
key_dimensions: Both 1861 and 1892 Acts retained official majority in all legislative councils — a non-negotiable British policy
Rationale: prevent any legislation unfavorable to British commercial or imperial interests
When official majority was first broken: provincial councils under GoI Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)
Central Legislature retained official majority until GoI Act 1935 — important chronological marker

concepts.name: Viceroy's Certifying Power and Overriding Authority (1861)
key_dimensions: Viceroy could certify a bill as essential for the safety/tranquility of British India, bypassing legislative council
This power made the legislative council advisory rather than truly legislative
Continuity of this principle in later acts: Governor-General's special powers under 1919 and 1935 Acts
Comparison with President's assent and withholding powers under the Indian Constitution

concepts.name: Separation of Executive and Legislative Functions (1861 Act)
key_dimensions: 1861 Act created a clear functional distinction: Executive Council governed, enlarged council legislated
Significance: precursor to the separation of powers doctrine in Indian constitutional evolution
Limitation: the Viceroy presided over both, so separation was functional not institutional
Contrast with GoI Act 1919 which introduced dyarchy — a more structural separation at provincial level

concepts.name: Composition of Central vs. Provincial Legislative Councils: Structural Comparison
key_dimensions: Central Legislative Council: Viceroy + Executive Council members + additional nominated members
Provincial Councils: Governor + Executive Council + additional nominated members (smaller in size)
Hierarchy: provincial councils could not legislate on matters reserved for central council
This two-tier structure as the embryonic form of the federal legislative hierarchy in India

concepts.name: Impact of 1857 Revolt on Constitutional Restructuring Leading to 1861 Act
key_dimensions: Transfer of power from East India Company to the British Crown (Government of India Act 1858) as the immediate precursor
Creation of Secretary of State for India and Council of India — how this changed the metropolitan oversight structure
Why 1861 Act was needed: reasserting British legislative authority, restoring administrative normalcy post-revolt
The 1861 Act as a conservative consolidation rather than a liberal reform — deliberate exclusion of broader Indian participation

concepts.name: Representational Gaps and Excluded Communities in 1861 and 1892 Acts
key_dimensions: Landlords, lawyers, and loyalist elites were the primary beneficiaries of nominated/recommended membership
Women, peasants, and lower castes were completely excluded — legislative councils represented elite opinion only
Communal representation not yet formalized (came with 1909 Act) but seeds of elite communal politics visible
Contrast with universal adult franchise introduced by the Indian Constitution in 1950

concepts.name: Significance of 1892 Act as a Bridge Between 1861 and Morley-Minto (1909)
key_dimensions: 1892 introduced quasi-representative principle; 1909 introduced communal electorate and actual elections — important progression
How each act responded to the political climate of its era: 1861 (post-revolt consolidation), 1892 (moderate nationalist pressure), 1909 (partition of Bengal agitation)
The incremental constitutional concession strategy of British imperialism — 'too little, too late' critique by nationalists
UPSC trap: placing reforms in wrong chronological sequence — 1861 → 1892 → 1909 → 1919 → 1935 must be memorized as a chain

concepts.name: Concept of 'Associations' and Recommendatory Bodies under 1892 Act
key_dimensions: Municipal corporations, district boards, universities, chambers of commerce, and zamindari associations were empowered to recommend members
These bodies represented propertied, educated, and commercial classes — class bias in representational design
The term 'recommendation' vs. 'election' — legal and political implications of this deliberate word choice
How this mechanism was a prototype for electoral colleges and indirect election concepts in later constitutional frameworks

concepts.name: Legislative Competence and Subject-Matter Jurisdiction of Councils (1861)
key_dimensions: Central Legislative Council had overriding legislative authority over provincial councils
Certain subjects (e.g., public debt, armed forces, relations with foreign states) were exclusively central
Provincial councils required Viceroy's prior approval for bills on specified sensitive matters
This subject-matter division as the historical foundation of the Union, State, and Concurrent List framework in later constitutions
